text:
REBAR!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! 
"What is Resizable BAR? Resizable BAR stands for Resizable Base Address Registers. It's an optimization technology that allows processors more effective access to VRAM memory on graphics cards. That in turn leads to performance upgrades for certain kinds of games, because it reduces CPU bottlenecking."

Without enabling REBAR from the bios this card is pretty poor. But with REBAR you almost double the performance. If you add late 13th gen CPU the ARC does wonders. Just don't use AMD as it has different architecture and the performance won't be optimum plus you are likely to get ghosting and glitches.

Drivers are already lot better. Still lot to go but the performance is there already for some titles to be played in 4k. This is turning to a cheap 4k entry level card. And why shouldn't it when the hardware is better than RX6800 or 4070ti. Also INTEL's next GPU launch Q4 2023 the drivers need to lot better by then so lot to come. 

I have always the same questions. Did you use AMD CPU? Did you enable REBAR?

text:
Not in the first generation they don't. Top performing flagship cards are great  for mind share, but they don't make up the bulk of sales. Most sales come from mid tier and lower graphics cards. Just look at the Steam hardware survey. Tons of GTX 1060s and 1050 Ti cards but a relatively lower percentage of higher end GPUs.

When Intel first launched the A750($280 MSRP) and A770($330 MSRP for the 8GB Model, $350 MSRP for the 16GB model), I believe they were targeting the then more expensive RTX 3050(around $300 or more at the time) and RTX 3060(closer to $400 at the time) respectively as far as performance and feature set were concerned. Basically, the idea was that Intel ARC would offer similar features and similar or better performance for less money. Now the price of the Nvidia cards have come down(3050 to around $260 on the low end, 3060 for $370 on the low end) but Arc hasn't dropped in price. In fact, it seems to have gone up in price, if it's available at all(pcpartpicker only shows prices for the A750 and it's up $10 at $290).

And that doesn't even factor in AMD. When the ARC A750 and A770 launched, you could already get an RX 6600 for like $240(faster than an RTX 3050) and an RX 6600 XT or 6650 XT  for around $300(generally faster than the 3060). For pure rasterization performance, ARC just didn't make sense for the price. And it's even worse for Intel now with the RX 6600 down to $190 and The 6650XT down to $250. And like this video mentioned, you can now get an RX 6700XT for $350(faster than an RTX 3060Ti for $400).
author: @jtenorj

text:
Intel now takes a look into DXVK, so that even real old (or Indie) DX9 games will work better. DXVK is used on Linux to play Windows-Games natively (without tinkering), but ARC can use it on Windows, too (at the moment very small manual tinkering needed). DXVK is a better let‘s call it „translater“ (a layer) to use the Vulkan API for DirectX and is much, much better than INTEL‘s own driver.As Vulkan is often so great itself (we all know Doom for example). 

Several tests proofed the power of DXVK on ARC (videos are easy to find in YT(. Kudos to Intel that they will look into it. That could be the game changer the Arc needs, like Rosetta is on Apple Silicon, that M1/M2 can „understand“ x32/x64 code, which allows the M1/M2 to use non-native programs to run so good (Microsoft will need this, too - I digress).

It is so great that Linux may be solves another problem in the Windows world hehe, as it already took over the internet, NAS etc. together with it‘s „relative“ BSD. Let‘s hope for the best.

Thanks TD for this little later ARC Video, but OBS usually works in the last iteration great with ARC - EposVox proofed overall better than NVENC, which is so great, as the new AMD Radeons will support AV1 good; another reason less to be prefer the green ones as many people missed the last improvements of the red cards. More will come as even CUDA has a harder and harder stand (still good used in quite some programs, but the predecessor will be open source).

Cheers, Pepe
